arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argued the statute requires explicit false statements. It cited the unchanged language from 1863.
The government argued a claim is fraudulent if it omits a known material breach. It cited the duty to disclose violations.
Justice Breyer questioned if common law contract principles apply to this statutory interpretation.
Justice Kagan posed a hypothetical involving an explicit contract term requiring doctor care.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the scope of the False Claims Act. It asks if a claim is false when it fails to disclose a known breach of a material contract term.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the boundary between a valid claim and a fraudulent one. It determines when silence about a breach constitutes fraud. The outcome shapes how companies report compliance to the government. It affects the financial liability of businesses in federal contracts.
